etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English, borrowed from Latin serēnus (“clear, cloudless, untroubled”).

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, “A Lady in Company”, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC, page 6:
quote.text: Serene, smiling, enigmatic, she faced him with no fear whatever showing in her dark eyes. The clear light of the bright autumn morning had no terrors for youth and health like hers.

definitions.definition: Without worry or anxiety; unaffected by disturbance.

quote.text: I took train and reached Wichita, where my active partner was awaiting me. He had just returned from the Medicine River, and reported everything serene.

definitions.definition: (archaic) Fair and unclouded (as of the sky); clear; unobscured.

quote.citation: 1717, Alexander Pope, “Winter. The Fourth Pastoral. […]”, in The Works of Mr. Alexander Pope, volume I, London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintot, […], →OCLC, page 30:
quote.text: Now ſleeping flocks on their ſoft fleeces lie, / The moon, ſerene in glory, mounts the sky,  […]

quote.citation: 1750 June 12 (date written; published 1751), T[homas] Gray, “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard”, in Designs by Mr. R[ichard] Bentley, for Six Poems by Mr. T. Gray, London:  […]  R[obert] Dodsley, […], published 1753, →OCLC, page 32:
quote.text: Full many a gem of pureſt ray ſerene / The dark unfathom'd caves of ocean bear:  […]

quote.citation: 1816 June – 1817 April/May (date written), [Mary Shelley], chapter VI, in Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London:  […]  [Macdonald and Son] for Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor, & Jones, published 1 January 1818, →OCLC:
quote.text: A serene sky and verdant fields filled me with ecstasy.

definitions.definition: Used as part of certain titles, originally to indicate sovereignty or independence.

quote.citation: 1708, [John Philips], “Book II”, in Cyder. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 68:
quote.text: The Hoary Froſts, and Northern Blaſts take care / Thy muddy Bev'rage to ſerene, and drive / Præcipitant the baſer, ropy Lees.

quote.citation: a. 1749 (date written), James Thomson, “Spring”, in The Seasons, London:  […]  A[ndrew] Millar, and sold by Thomas Cadell, […], published 1768, →OCLC, page 34, lines 866–867:
quote.text: When heaven and earth, as if contending, vye / To raiſe his being, and ſerene his ſoul.

quote.citation: 1801, Robert Southey, “(please specify the page)”, in Thalaba the Destroyer, volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London:  […]  [F]or T[homas] N[orton] Longman and O[wen] Rees, […], by Biggs and Cottle, […], →OCLC:
1742, Edward Young, Night Thoughts on Life, Death and Immortality:
quote.text: To their master is denied / To share their sweet serene.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Middle French serein, from Old French serein (“evening”), from Vulgar Latin *serānum, from substantive use of sērum, neuter of sērus (“late”) + -ānus suffix.

definitions.definition: A fine rain from a cloudless sky after sunset.

quote.citation: 1605 (first performance), Ben[jamin] Jonson, Ben: Ionson His Volpone or The Foxe, [London]:  […]  [George Eld] for Thomas Thorppe, published 1607, →OCLC, Act III, scene vii, signatures H2, recto – H2, verso:
quote.text: Some ſerene blaſt me, or dire lightning ſtrike / This my offending face.
